questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A property sells for $280,000 and the listing agreement specifies a 6% commission. What is the total commission?

explanations.b: $28,000 equals 10% of the sale price, not 6%.
explanations.c: $1,680 results from multiplying by 0.006 instead of 0.06.
explanations.d: $14,000 equals 5% of the sale price, not 6%.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A property sells for $350,000 at a 6% commission split equally between the listing and selling broker. Each salesperson receives 60% of her broker's share. How much does the listing salesperson earn?

explanations.a: $21,000 is the total commission, not the individual salesperson's share.
explanations.c: $10,500 is the listing broker's full share before splitting with the salesperson.
explanations.d: $12,600 would be 60% of the entire commission, not 60% of the listing broker's half.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.keyword: sale price to yield target net
questions.text: A seller nets $226,800 after paying a 5.5% commission. What was the sale price?

explanations.a: $239,274 is not the correct result; sale price = net ÷ (1 − rate).

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7B Valuation, market sale price, and yields
questions.keyword: value from NOI and required cap rate
questions.text: An investor requires a 7% cap rate on a property generating $63,000 in annual net operating income. What maximum price should the investor pay?

explanations.a: $441,000 results from multiplying NOI × 7 rather than dividing: $63,000 × 7 = $441,000.
explanations.c: $63,000 is the NOI itself, not a property value derived from it.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7B Valuation, market sale price, and yields
questions.text: A rental home generates $1,500 per month in gross rent. Properties in the area sell at a gross rent multiplier (GRM) of 120. What is the estimated value?

explanations.a: Value = monthly rent × GRM = $1,500 × 120 = $180,000.
explanations.b: $125,000 does not result from the given figures using the GRM formula.
explanations.c: $15,000 results from applying a GRM of 10 rather than 120: $1,500 × 10 = $15,000.
explanations.d: $18,000 is the annual gross rent ($1,500 × 12) without applying the GRM.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7C Net to seller, cost to buyer
questions.keyword: seller net after commission and mortgage
questions.text: A seller sells her home for $325,000, pays a 6% commission, and has an outstanding mortgage of $198,000. What are her approximate net proceeds?

explanations.a: $127,000 ignores the commission; it equals $325,000 − $198,000 only.
explanations.c: $121,000 does not correspond to the correct deduction sequence.
explanations.d: $325,000 is the gross sale price before any deductions.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7C Net to seller, cost to buyer
questions.keyword: buyer cash to close points and down payment
questions.text: A buyer makes a $4,800 down payment and pays 1.5 discount points on a $240,000 mortgage. What is the total cash required at closing for these two items?

explanations.a: $7,200 uses only 1 point (1% × $240,000 = $2,400) plus the $4,800 down payment.
explanations.b: $9,600 uses 2 points ($4,800) plus the $4,800 down payment, overstating the points.
explanations.d: $4,800 is the down payment only; the $3,600 cost of the points is omitted.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7C Net to seller, cost to buyer
questions.keyword: down payment plus origination fee total
questions.text: A buyer purchases a $300,000 home with a 10% down payment and a 1% loan origination fee on the loan amount. What is the total of the down payment plus origination fee?

explanations.a: $33,000 applies 1% to the full purchase price ($3,000) rather than the loan amount ($2,700), then adds the down payment.
explanations.b: $30,000 is the down payment alone (10% × $300,000), ignoring the origination fee.
explanations.c: $30,300 applies 1% to the down payment ($300) rather than the loan — a common base error.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: Annual property taxes are $3,650. What is the daily proration amount using a 365-day year?

explanations.a: Daily rate = $3,650 ÷ 365 = $10.00 per day.
explanations.b: $304.17 is the monthly rate ($3,650 ÷ 12), not the daily rate.
explanations.c: $365.00 per day would require annual taxes of $133,225.
explanations.d: $1.00 per day would mean annual taxes of only $365.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.keyword: seller tax proration credit months owned
questions.text: Closing occurs on April 30. Annual property taxes of $3,600 are unpaid. Using 30-day months, how much does the seller owe the buyer as a tax proration?

explanations.a: $300 equals one month's taxes; the seller owned the property for four months (January through April).
explanations.b: Monthly tax = $3,600 ÷ 12 = $300. Seller's four months = $300 × 4 = $1,200.
explanations.c: $2,400 represents eight months — the buyer's share, not the seller's.
explanations.d: $3,600 is the full annual tax; only the seller's proportionate share is prorated.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.keyword: prepaid rent buyer credit at closing
questions.text: Closing occurs on June 10. The tenant has already paid the full June rent of $1,500. Using a 30-day month, how much rent is credited to the buyer at closing?

explanations.a: $500 = 10 days × $50 — this is the seller's portion (June 1–10), not the buyer's.
explanations.b: $750 = 15 days × $50, using an incorrect half-month assumption rather than the actual closing date.
explanations.c: Daily rent = $1,500 ÷ 30 = $50. Buyer's days = June 11–30 = 20 days. Credit = 20 × $50 = $1,000.
explanations.d: $1,100 = 22 days × $50 — off by two days from the correct buyer day count.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A borrower has a $180,000 outstanding mortgage balance at 6% annual interest. What is the interest portion of the next monthly payment?

explanations.a: $10,800 = $180,000 × 6% is the annual interest; the monthly amount requires dividing by 12.
explanations.b: $1,800 results from applying a 12% rate (double the stated rate) to the balance and dividing by 12.
explanations.c: $1,080 results from dividing the annual interest ($10,800) by 10 instead of 12.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A borrower's monthly payment is $1,150, and the interest portion for the month is $750. How much of the payment reduces the principal balance?

explanations.a: Principal reduction = total payment − interest = $1,150 − $750 = $400.
explanations.b: $1,900 is the sum of the payment and interest, not the difference.
explanations.c: $800 is twice the correct answer, a common doubling error.
explanations.d: $1,150 is the total payment, not the portion reducing principal.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.keyword: discount points dollar cost at closing
questions.text: A lender charges 2.5 discount points on a $200,000 mortgage. What is the dollar cost of those points at closing?

explanations.a: $2,500 is the cost of 1.25 points, not 2.5 points.
explanations.b: One point = 1% of the loan. 2.5 points = 2.5% × $200,000 = $5,000.
explanations.c: $4,000 = 2% × $200,000, confusing 2 points with 2.5 points.
explanations.d: $25,000 would be 12.5% of the loan, far more than 2.5 points.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A borrower pays $3,600 in discount points to reduce her monthly payment by $30. Approximately how many months will it take to recover the cost of the points?

explanations.a: 18 months would imply savings of $200 per month ($3,600 ÷ 18); actual savings are only $30.
explanations.b: 360 months (30 years) would imply savings of $10 per month; actual savings are $30.
explanations.c: Break-even = cost ÷ monthly savings = $3,600 ÷ $30 = 120 months (10 years).
explanations.d: 30 months would imply savings of $120 per month; actual savings are $30.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A mortgage note carries a prepayment penalty of 2% of the outstanding balance if paid off within the first three years. A borrower pays off a $150,000 balance in year two. What is the penalty?

explanations.a: $2,000 would result from applying 2% to a $100,000 balance, not the actual $150,000.
explanations.b: $150 = 0.1% of $150,000 — a decimal-point error in the 2% rate.
explanations.c: $1,500 = 1% × $150,000, applying half the stated penalty rate.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A lender approves a loan at 80% LTV on a $275,000 purchase. What is the required down payment?

explanations.a: Down payment = purchase × (1 − LTV) = $275,000 × 20% = $55,000.
explanations.b: $220,000 is the loan amount (80% × $275,000), not the down payment.
explanations.c: $27,500 = 10% of the price, corresponding to a 90% LTV loan.
explanations.d: $275,000 is the full purchase price, not the down payment.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A property is appraised at $300,000 and the outstanding mortgage balance is $225,000. The lender requires PMI when LTV exceeds 80%. Does this homeowner currently need PMI?

answers.text: Yes, because any loan balance over $200,000 requires PMI regardless of property value
No, because the LTV is 75%, which is below the 80% PMI threshold
Yes, because the original down payment was likely under 20%
No, because PMI is required only on FHA-insured loans

explanations.a: PMI is based on the current LTV ratio, not on an absolute loan balance dollar threshold.
explanations.b: LTV = $225,000 ÷ $300,000 = 75%. Since 75% is below the 80% trigger, PMI is not currently required.
explanations.c: What matters for current PMI status is the present LTV, not the original down payment percentage.
explanations.d: Conventional lenders — not just FHA — require PMI when LTV exceeds 80%; the trigger is the LTV ratio, not the loan type.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A property appraises at $400,000 and the buyer requests a $340,000 loan. What is the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio?

explanations.a: 117.6% results from dividing value by loan ($400,000 ÷ $340,000), the inverse of LTV.
explanations.b: 60% is not the result of $340,000 ÷ $400,000.
explanations.c: LTV = loan ÷ appraised value = $340,000 ÷ $400,000 = 85%.
explanations.d: 15% is the equity percentage (1 − LTV), not the LTV ratio.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: An L-shaped room divides into two rectangles: 20 ft × 15 ft and 10 ft × 12 ft. What is the total square footage?

explanations.a: 300 sq ft is only the larger rectangle (20 × 15); the smaller section is omitted.
explanations.b: 120 sq ft is only the smaller rectangle (10 × 12); the larger section is omitted.
explanations.c: 540 sq ft results from treating the shape as one large rectangle of 20 × 27, incorrectly adding depths.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A parcel measures 1,320 feet by 330 feet. How many acres does it contain? (1 acre = 43,560 sq ft)

explanations.b: 43,560 is square feet per acre — the divisor, not the acreage result.
explanations.c: 5 acres = 217,800 sq ft; this parcel at 435,600 sq ft is twice that size.
explanations.d: 20 acres = 871,200 sq ft; this parcel is half that size.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.text: A room measures 20 feet long, 15 feet wide, and 9 feet high. What is its volume in cubic feet?

explanations.a: 300 cubic feet is the floor area (20 × 15) without multiplying by ceiling height.
explanations.b: Volume = 20 × 15 × 9 = 2,700 cubic feet.
explanations.c: 180 cubic feet results from adding the three dimensions instead of multiplying them.
explanations.d: 27,000 cubic feet is ten times the correct volume.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7J Property management, investment, rate of return
questions.text: A rental property has annual gross rents of $72,000, a 5% vacancy rate, and operating expenses of $28,000. What is the net operating income (NOI)?

explanations.a: $44,000 = $72,000 − $28,000, which omits the vacancy deduction.
explanations.b: $68,400 is the effective gross income after vacancy ($72,000 × 95%), but operating expenses have not yet been deducted.
explanations.d: $72,000 is the potential gross income before any vacancy or expense deductions.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7J Property management, investment, rate of return
questions.text: An investor contributes $50,000 cash and receives $4,500 in annual pre-tax cash flow after all expenses and debt service. What is the cash-on-cash return?

explanations.a: 11.1% results from inverting the formula: $50,000 ÷ $4,500 ≈ 11.1 — dividing equity by income instead of income by equity.
explanations.b: 0.9% misplaces the decimal; $4,500 ÷ $50,000 = 0.09 = 9%, not 0.9%.
explanations.c: 4.5% would result if the equity invested were $100,000 rather than $50,000.
explanations.d: Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow ÷ cash invested = $4,500 ÷ $50,000 = 9%.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.keyword: minimum sale price for net target
questions.text: A seller wants to net $190,000 after paying a 5% commission. What is the minimum sale price needed?

explanations.c: $199,500 × 5% = $9,975; net = $189,525, still below the target.
explanations.d: $209,500 × 5% = $10,475; net = $199,025, which exceeds the target unnecessarily.

questions.name: Real Estate Calculations
questions.objective: 7B Valuation, market sale price, and yields
questions.text: An office building sold for $1,200,000 and produces $96,000 in annual net operating income. What is the implied capitalization rate?

explanations.a: 12.5% would imply a sale price of $768,000 ($96,000 ÷ 0.125), lower than the actual $1,200,000.
explanations.b: Cap rate = NOI ÷ sale price = $96,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 8%.
explanations.c: 80% results from dividing the sale price by the NOI instead of NOI by price.
explanations.d: A 4% cap rate would imply a sale price of $2,400,000 for the same NOI.
